Reviewed state: branch `docs/cross-agent-reviewers` at `515a1eb` (identical to `main`; no commits on the branch), one unstaged modification to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` replacing the three-line note after step 12 with a `### The reviewers steps 6-8 invoke` subsection. Nothing staged, nothing untracked (`.entire/` is ignored). No code, test, or build changes — so no C/CMake surface to review.

The intent is right and the prose is good. What blocks it is that the central instruction — "use your own harness's sub-agents" — asserts a capability it does not define, and the "commit it" instruction collides with two other steps in the same file.

### Findings

**1. Should-fix — `AGENTS.md:220-221`: the bullet asserts every harness has sub-agents but never says what the mechanism actually is, so a non-Claude agent cannot act on it.**
"Codex, Cursor and others have an equivalent; use it" is the load-bearing sentence of the whole change, and it is the one sentence that carries no instruction. Cursor has custom agents; Codex CLI has no project-scoped sub-agent definition at all — its equivalent is a fresh non-interactive session (`codex exec`) handed the reviewer prompt. A Codex agent reading this looks for a "sub-agent" feature, finds none, and falls straight through to bullet three — producing exactly the self-review outcome the change exists to prevent. Fix: define the mechanism portably rather than by brand name, e.g. *"a reviewer is a fresh session that has your reviewer instructions and the diff and nothing else — a sub-agent if your harness has them, otherwise a second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI (`codex exec` and equivalents). A new session reading the diff cold satisfies this; the same session in a new turn does not."* That both makes it actionable and shrinks bullet three to near-unreachable.

**2. Should-fix — `AGENTS.md:227-231`: "commit it" conflicts with step 3, step 10 and step 8.**
As written, an agent that creates `.codex/agents/code-review.md` mid-feature commits it on the feature branch — that is combining unrelated work (`AGENTS.md:187`) and breaks the thin vertical slice (step 3). Worse, step 8 requires `code-review` before *every* commit, and the commit in question is the one creating that reviewer: the bootstrap cannot satisfy the rule. Fix: say the definition lands as its own change — its own branch and `chore(agents): ...` commit, before the work it will review — and state explicitly that this first commit is the one legitimate self-review, disclosed as such.

**3. Should-fix — `AGENTS.md:222-226`: telling each harness to restate the role definitions contradicts this file's own premise and guarantees drift.**
`AGENTS.md:3-5` exists precisely so rules are not duplicated per tool ("keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing"), and the bullet itself names drift as the danger — then prescribes three copies of the same spec. It also demonstrates the drift in miniature: the summary here says `code-review` is "an expert in C17 and CMake" (the real file adds terminal/CLI game programming and requires an explicit approve/request-changes verdict plus untracked-file coverage) and that `verifier` "runs the builds and tests" (the real file mandates both build types, `ctest`, `tests/tui.sh` and the golden fixtures). Fix: make `.claude/agents/*.md` the single source and have the per-tool definition be a pointer — *"read `.claude/agents/<name>.md` and follow it"* — carrying only the harness-specific wiring (name, read-only). This also answers the vendor-directory worry directly: a three-line pointer file for a tool the owner does not use is cheap and does not rot, where a duplicated spec is neither.

**4. Should-fix — `AGENTS.md:232-236`: the escape hatch is not falsifiable, and its disclosure rule is narrower than step 9's.**
"Only if the harness *genuinely* has no sub-agents" is exhortation, not a test an agent can fail. And disclosure is required only "in the pull request", while most of this review happens before a PR exists; step 9 already sets the house pattern at `AGENTS.md:173-177` ("in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request"). "Each begun fresh" is also undefined for a harness that cannot clear its own context. Fix: require the agent to name the mechanism it checked for and why it was unavailable; mirror step 9's dual disclosure wording; and replace "begun fresh" with the concrete requirement the opening paragraph already states — conclusions reached from the diff, not from memory of intent.

**5. Nit — `AGENTS.md:238-241`: "every issue in the tracker refer to these three by name" is an overclaim.**
Exactly one issue does (#66); two commits do (`515a1eb`, `9b3e5b2`). A verifiably false supporting clause weakens a rule that is otherwise correct. "the workflow above, the commit history and the issue tracker refer to these three by name" is both true and enough.

**6. Nit — `AGENTS.md:209`: the heading hard-codes step numbers and needs a relative pronoun.**
Open issue #65 is about workflow numbering drift, and the numbering just shifted in `515a1eb` when step 9 was inserted; a heading is the worst place to embed a number, since anchors break with it. "The reviewers steps 6-8 invoke" also stumbles without "that". Suggest a stable noun phrase such as `### The review sub-agents`, with the step numbers left in the body.

**7. Nit — no forward pointer from steps 6-8 to the new section (`AGENTS.md:123-141`).**
Step 5 sets the precedent with "see step 9" (`AGENTS.md:121`). A non-Claude agent reading step 6 sees only "invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent"; the section that tells it what that means for its harness is 90 lines further down, after the numbered list ends. One clause on step 6 fixes it.

**8. Nit — repetition (`AGENTS.md:211-215`, `235-236`, `238-241`).** The same idea — a reader who did not write the work — is made three times. Length itself is fine and in proportion to neighbours (step 9 is 35 lines, the tmux bullet 17), but roughly five lines could go without losing an instruction.

### Not reviewed

I could not test the central assumption — that a Codex or Cursor agent will read an agent definition committed under `.codex/` or `.cursor/`. Neither harness is available here, and the in-repo `.codex/` and `.cursor/` contain only `entire` hook configuration, no agent definitions, so there is no precedent in the tree to confirm the path. Finding 3's pointer-file approach reduces the cost of getting that path wrong, but it does not verify it; the section should ideally require the author to confirm the harness actually loads the file, since a definition in a directory the tool never reads is inert while reading as if the step were done.

input.old_string:
### The reviewers steps 6-8 invoke

Those three steps invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in
`.claude/agents/`: `ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. The point of
them is not the tool — it is that the work is judged by a reader who did
not write it, and who has to reach its conclusions from the diff rather
than from a memory of having intended something.

An agent that is not Claude Code gets those three passes the same way, and
does not skip them:

- **Use your own harness's sub-agents.** Codex, Cursor and others have an
  equivalent; use it. Give each reviewer the same role, the same name, and
  the same read-only rule as the definitions in `.claude/agents/`, which
  are the reference: `ui-review` is an expert in games and CLI games,
  `verifier` runs the builds and tests, `code-review` is an expert in C17
  and CMake, and none of the three may edit a file. They report, and the
  main agent fixes.
- **Write the definition down where your harness reads it,** beside the
  configuration it already keeps there — this repository has `.codex/` and
  `.cursor/` — and commit it, so the next session in that tool inherits a
  reviewer instead of improvising one. A reviewer that has to be invented
  each time is a reviewer that drifts.
- **Only if the harness genuinely has no sub-agents,** review it yourself
  in three separate passes, each begun fresh, and say plainly in the pull
  request that the review was self-administered. That is the weakest form
  of this step: the reader and the author share a memory, which is exactly
  the thing a reviewer is for.

Keeping the names identical matters more than it looks: the workflow above,
the commit history and every issue in the tracker refer to these three by
name, and a `code-review` that means something different per tool makes all
of that unreadable.

### The review sub-agents

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

An agent that is not Claude Code gets the same three passes, and does not
skip them.

- **A reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the
  change, and nothing else.** A sub-agent where the harness has them; a
  second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI — `codex exec` and its
  equivalents — where it does not. A new session reading the change cold
  satisfies this. The same session in a later turn does not.
- **Point at the definitions here rather than restating them.**
  `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are the
  specifications. A per-tool definition should say to read the matching
  file and follow it, and carry only the wiring its own harness needs: the
  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the
  text is how three tools come to review three different things, which is
  the whole reason this file exists.
- **Keep the three names.** The workflow above, the commit history and the
  issue tracker all refer to them by name.
- **Land the definition as its own change,** on its own branch and commit,
  before the work it will review — not beside a feature, which step 10
  forbids and step 3 argues against. That commit is the one place
  self-review cannot be avoided, since step 8 cannot be satisfied by the
  commit that creates the reviewer. Say so in it.
- **Confirm the harness actually loads what you wrote.** A definition in a
  directory the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside it looks
  exactly like a step that was carried out.
- **Self-review is the last resort, not the default.** Taking it means
  saying which mechanism you looked for and why it was not there, in the
  pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone
  when there is no pull request. A reviewer who shares the author's memory
  of what was intended is the one thing this section exists to prevent.

input.command:
tests/instructions.sh . && git add AGENTS.md && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --format='%G? %h %s' -1
docs: have every agent get its review from a reader, not itself

The workflow's three review passes ran on Claude Code sub-agents, and the
only thing said to any other agent was a line at the end telling it to
perform the equivalent passes itself. That is the weakest possible
reading of a review: the author and the reader share a memory of what was
intended, which is the one thing a reviewer is for.

An agent that is not Claude Code now gets the same three passes. The
mechanism is stated in a way any harness can act on -- a reviewer is a
fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the change, and
nothing else, which is a sub-agent where the harness has them and a
second non-interactive invocation of its own CLI where it does not. A new
session reading the change cold satisfies it; the same session a turn
later does not.

The per-tool definition points at `.claude/agents/` rather than restating
it. Three copies of a specification are three specifications, which is
what this file exists to prevent -- and the first draft proved the point
by describing code-review as a C17 and CMake expert while its definition
also asks for terminal game expertise and an explicit verdict.

It lands as its own change, before the work it will review, because a
reviewer committed beside a feature is the unrelated work step 10
forbids, and because step 8 cannot be satisfied by the commit that
creates the reviewer -- the one place self-review is unavoidable, and it
has to say so.

Self-review survives only as a last resort, and taking it means naming
the mechanism looked for and why it was not there.

Nothing here claims a path into `.codex/` or `.cursor/`. Those hold hook
configuration and nothing either tool reads agent definitions from, so
the rule asks the author to confirm the harness loads what they wrote: a
definition somewhere the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside
looks exactly like a step that was carried out.
